readingInstruction: Read Daniel 9:1-10:21. Daniel reads Jeremiah, prays one of the greatest prayers of confession in the Bible, and receives the prophecy of the seventy weeks. Then a vision of a glorious man and a message from an angel who was delayed by spiritual conflict. Read the prayer first, and take your time.
settingTheScene: Chapter 9 is dated to 539 BC, the first year of Darius. Daniel, now an old man, reads Jeremiah’s prophecy of seventy years (Jeremiah 25:11-12; 29:10), and realizes that the time is near. He responds by prayer. Chapter 10 is dated three years later, in 536 BC. Daniel is mourning and fasting when he sees a vision of a man in linen, and receives a message about the conflict between spiritual powers.
observation: “I, Daniel, perceived in the books the number of years that, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, must pass before the end of the desolations of Jerusalem” (9:2).
“Then I turned my face to the Lord God, seeking him by prayer and pleas for mercy with fasting and sackcloth and ashes” (9:3).
“We have sinned and done wrong and acted wickedly and rebelled, turning aside from your commandments” (9:5).
“To the Lord our God belong mercy and forgiveness, for we have rebelled against him” (9:9).
“For we do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy” (9:18).
“O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive. O Lord, pay attention and act. For your own sake, O my God, do not delay” (9:19).
“Seventy weeks are decreed about your people and your holy city, to finish the transgression, to put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness” (9:24).
“Fear not, Daniel, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and humbled yourself before your God, your words have been heard” (10:12).
interpretation:
Daniel’s prayer is a model. He begins with God’s word: he has read the book and trusts the promise. But the promise leads him to pray, not to relax. He knows that God’s promises are fulfilled in the context of repentance. He fasts and confesses, using the first person plural, “we have sinned,” though Daniel himself is portrayed as blameless. He identifies with the people. He praises God as great and awesome, keeping covenant and steadfast love. He admits that the curses of Moses have fallen because of their disobedience.

Notice what he does not argue. He does not appeal to his own righteousness or to Israel’s merits. “We do not present our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy.” The appeal is for God’s name’s sake. The prayer is urgent: “O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive; O Lord, pay attention and act.”

The answer comes by Gabriel, who says that as soon as Daniel began to pray, a word went out. Then the prophecy of the seventy weeks: seventy sevens decreed for the people and the city. Six things are to be accomplished: to finish the transgression, to put an end to sin, to atone for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal the vision and prophecy, and to anoint a most holy place. These are the great goals of redemption. The details of the timeline are debated, but Christians have long seen in it a pointer to the Messiah, the anointed one, who will be cut off and bring the atonement.

Chapter 10 shows a heavenly dimension. Daniel’s prayer had been heard from the first day, but the angel was delayed 21 days by “the prince of the kingdom of Persia” until Michael came to help. This is a glimpse of spiritual warfare behind the scenes of history. Daniel is strengthened by the angel’s touch: “Peace be with you; be strong and of good courage.”
connection: 1 John 1:9 says, “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins.” Romans 5:6-11 speaks of Christ dying for the ungodly. Hebrews 9:26 says Christ has appeared “to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself,” fulfilling the goals of Daniel 9:24. Ephesians 6:12 says we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the spiritual forces of evil. Revelation 1:12-18 shows the glorified Christ in a similar picture to Daniel 10.
application:
Use Daniel’s prayer as a pattern. Start with God’s word, confess honestly, appeal to his mercy and not your merit.

Pray for your community or nation, using “we” and not “they.”

Take courage from Daniel 10:12. Your prayers are heard from the first day, even if the answer is delayed.
prayerPrompts: Confess your sin and the sin of your people in your own words.
Tell God you do not plead your righteousness but his mercy.
Ask him to hear and act for his own name’s sake.
